venues.d: A palatial tower on the highest of the White City's seven hills — Four Seasons polish, the surest hands in Jordan.
Butler service on every floor and Levantine art throughout — the St. Regis ritual, brought to the diplomatic quarter.
A glass tower over the new downtown — floor-to-ceiling city views, Le Labo baths, beside the Four Seasons and St. Regis.
A long-standing grand house near Rainbow Street — an in-house art gallery and four restaurants, quietly reliable.
A bold contemporary statement in the new downtown — a canyon-walk entrance inspired by Petra, and W's design energy.
Nine pools and hanging gardens down to the shore — a Babylon-inspired resort on the longest private beach in Jordan.
Glass-domed 'Martian' bubble suites open to the stars, deep in the Valley of the Moon — the desert night, in comfort.
Farm-to-table Jordanian home cooking in a sunlit old house — the freshest, most honest table in the city.
Lebanese fine dining in a former prime minister's villa — immaculate mezze and service, the grand Amman institution since 1997.
Chef Ali Ghzawi's modern Levantine cooking — home flavours retold through storytelling and playful texture.
Season-led cooking with an Italian thread, in a beautifully restored villa — the most talked-about opening in the city.
Traditional Jordanian cooking in a converted 1950s villa with a garden terrace — the classic Amman lunch.
The city's iconic falafel-and-hummus house since the 1950s — open all hours, once served the royal family, still unbeatable.
'Grandmother's house' — a hands-on home-cooking experience in a restored family home, cooking then sharing the meal.
A rooftop of found-object 'junk' art and open-air seating — quirky Jordanian plates over the old city's lights.

The 1.2km sandstone gorge that opens Petra: walls soaring 80 metres, narrowing to a slit, until the Treasury flashes into view at the end. Walk it slowly at first light with a private guide before the coaches arrive, and let the children run the last stretch to the reveal.

The single most recognisable facade on earth, 40 metres of rose-red rock carved straight into the cliff by the Nabataeans. Arrive at dawn for the light on the columns and space for a proper family photograph, then take mint tea at a cliffside spot facing it.

Petra's largest monument, wider and taller than the Treasury, reached by roughly 800 rock-cut steps high into the mountains. Well worth a second day; older travellers can ride a donkey up while the fit hike, and the view from the ridge opposite is the reward.

A row of grand mausoleums carved into the cliff below the theatre — the Urn, Silk, Corinthian and Palace tombs — their stone banded in swirls of colour. Climb at late afternoon when the west light sets the whole facade glowing.

venues.n: The High Place of Sacrifice, Petra
venues.d: A Nabataean altar platform on a summit reached by a stepped trail, with a sweeping view over the entire valley of tombs. A rewarding morning climb for active families; a guide brings the ritual carvings to life.

venues.n: The Street of Facades & Colonnaded Street, Petra
venues.d: Beyond the Treasury the canyon widens into a whole carved city — rows of tomb facades, a Roman theatre cut from rock, and a colonnaded main street. This is where a full day inside Petra earns its keep, ideally at an unhurried pace with a driver waiting at the gate.

Three or four evenings a week the Siq is lit by some 1,500 candles and you walk in near-silence to the Treasury for music and story under the stars. A quietly magical close to a Petra day; book ahead and go on a night your camp or hotel can arrange transfers.

A miniature Nabataean canyon a short drive north of Petra, far quieter, with a rare painted ceiling in one of its rock-cut halls. A gentle, crowd-free hour that pairs beautifully with a long lunch at one of the boutique lodges nearby.

On the city's highest hill, layered with Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad remains and a grandstand view over the white houses of Amman. The obvious first stop; a private guide turns the scattered stones into a clear story for three generations at once.

Two towering Roman columns and a giant carved stone hand are all that remain of a 2nd-century temple that would have outsized anything in Rome. Golden hour here, with the city falling away below, is one of Amman's finest photographs.

An 8th-century audience hall crowned by a reconstructed dome, the most photogenic corner of the Citadel and cool inside on a hot afternoon. The domed chamber and vast underground cistern reward a slow look with someone who can explain them.

A 6,000-seat theatre cut into the hillside in the 2nd century, still steeply dramatic in the heart of downtown. Climb to the top row for the view; the two small folklore museums flanking it are a quick, worthwhile add.

Jordan's flagship museum in Ras al-Ayn, home to the 9,000-year-old Ain Ghazal statues — among the oldest large human figures ever made — and copper-scroll material from the Dead Sea Scrolls. Air-conditioned, beautifully laid out and ideal for a hot midday with children.

Amman's landmark mosque, its vast blue mosaic dome visible across the city, built 1982–89 and open to respectful non-Muslim visitors outside prayer times. A serene, cool interior; robes are provided and a discreet guide smooths the visit for a family.

The city's most walkable stretch — cafes, galleries and rooftop views on Rainbow Street, spice, gold and textile souks tumbling downhill into Al-Balad. Best explored on foot late afternoon; a good private guide knows which lanes are worth the detour.

Some 70-plus cars and motorcycles from the late King Hussein's collection, from a 1916 Cadillac of the Arab Revolt to a Mercedes gullwing, a Ferrari F40 and the Aston Martin. A genuine crowd-pleaser for car-loving teenagers and grandfathers alike, set in King Hussein Park.

A hillside compound of restored 1920s houses and a small Byzantine ruin, now Amman's leading home for Arab contemporary art, with gardens, a library and a quiet cafe overlooking the old city. A calm, cultured hour away from the heat and crowds.

venues.n: The Jara Souk & Wild Jordan Center, Amman
venues.d: The Friday Souk Jara for local craft and the RSCN's Wild Jordan cafe for one of the city's best terrace views and honest Jordanian cooking. Both are easy, characterful stops; Wild Jordan is reliably good for vegetarian and Jain-aware family dining.

Two Amman institutions minutes apart: Hashem for 24-hour falafel, hummus and fatteh in a downtown alley, and Habibah since 1951 for the definitive plate of warm kunafa. The most authentic bite in the city — and both are naturally vegetarian-friendly.

A private jeep tour across the red sand of the Valley of the Moon — towering rock walls, dunes, springs and canyons that doubled as Mars on film. The essential Wadi Rum half-day; camel or horse can be added for the children.

venues.n: A Night in a Luxury Bedouin Camp, Wadi Rum
venues.d: Sleep in a domed or Martian-style suite with a private terrace, a zarb dinner cooked underground, and a sky thick with stars. The finest camps offer proper beds, ensuite bathrooms and discreet service — an unforgettable, safe night out for multi-generation families.

venues.n: Um Fruth & Burdah Rock Bridges, Wadi Rum
venues.d: Two natural stone arches — the low, climbable Um Fruth and the lofty Burdah, one of the highest rock bridges anywhere. Um Fruth is an easy scramble for a family photo; Burdah is a guided half-day for the surefooted.

venues.n: Khazali Canyon & Lawrence's Spring, Wadi Rum
venues.d: A cool, shaded slot canyon walled with ancient Thamudic petroglyphs, and the greenery of a spring tied to T.E. Lawrence. Gentle, atmospheric stops on a jeep route — the carvings fascinate children when a Bedouin guide reads them.

A sunrise flight above the desert, drifting over red dunes and sandstone islands as the light turns them gold. The most serene view of Rum there is — a private basket can be arranged for a special morning.

With almost no light pollution, Rum is among the world's great skies; camps run telescope sessions on the Milky Way and planets, best around the new moon. A quiet, wondrous close to a desert day for all ages.

Bob effortlessly on the surface of the lowest point on earth, 430-odd metres below sea level, water so salt-dense you cannot sink. A must-do novelty for the whole family; go from a resort beach with fresh-water showers close by.

Coat yourself in mineral-black mud, let it dry, rinse it off in the sea, then retreat to a world-class spa — the Kempinski Ishtar's is among the largest in the Middle East. A restorative day of pampering for multi-generation travellers.

One of the best-preserved Roman provincial cities anywhere — the colonnaded Oval Plaza, an 800-metre chariot-rutted Cardo, the Temple of Artemis, Hadrian's Arch and a hippodrome. A day trip from Amman that astonishes; a guide and an early start make it.

In a working Greek Orthodox church, the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land — a 6th-century floor mosaic of some two million tiles. Small but extraordinary; Madaba's mosaic workshops and stone-set churches fill a rewarding half-day.

The height from which Moses is said to have seen the Promised Land, with a fine memorial church, ancient mosaics and a view stretching to the Dead Sea and, on a clear day, Jerusalem. A moving, easy stop near Madaba for any family.

venues.n: Bethany Beyond the Jordan (The Baptism Site)
venues.d: The believed site of Christ's baptism on the east bank of the Jordan — excavated churches, pools and the riverbank itself. A serene, deeply meaningful visit; access is by official shuttle with a guide, so plan through your concierge.

Jordan's largest reserve, tumbling from cool mountains to desert lowlands across four ecological zones, with over 800 plant species and rare Nubian ibex. Hike the Wadi Dana trail or simply take the sunset view; a wild, restorative counterpoint to the ruins.

A candlelit, solar-run lodge at the desert end of Dana, named among the world's top eco-lodges by National Geographic, reached the last stretch by Bedouin 4x4. Star-bathed nights, Bedouin hospitality and slow days — a rare, soulful stay for the curious.

The Red Sea at Aqaba holds warm, clear water year-round, healthy coral and famous sites like the sunken tank and the Cedar Pride wreck within a protected marine park. Gentle house reefs suit first-time snorkellers and children; private boat dives suit the certified.

Jordan's warm-water resort town on the Gulf of Aqaba, the natural place to unwind after Petra and Wadi Rum with beach clubs, glass-bottom boats and easy family swimming. A relaxed coda to a Jordan itinerary, with views across to three countries.

A square, near-perfect Umayyad building in the open desert, long thought a fort but likely a caravan inn, its rooms ranged around a courtyard. A striking, atmospheric stop on the eastern loop — quick to see and photogenic against empty land.

A black-basalt fortress rebuilt in the 13th century and famous as T.E. Lawrence's winter headquarters during the Arab Revolt. History buffs and Lawrence readers relish it; pair with the nearby Azraq wetland reserve.

A Decapolis city on a green plateau in Jordan's far north, its black-and-white theatre and colonnaded street looking out over the Sea of Galilee and the Golan. Panoramic, uncrowded and lovely at sunset, with a well-regarded local restaurant on site.

A 12th-century Ayyubid fortress raised under Saladin to face the Crusaders, commanding wooded hills and long views over the Jordan Valley. A satisfying stop for children who like castles, often paired with Jerash and Umm Qais on a northern day.

A honey-limestone Ottoman-era town on three hills, famed for its yellow-stone mansions and a lived tradition of Muslim-Christian harmony. A gentle, authentic half-day of stepped lanes and guest-house hospitality, a short drive from Amman.

A quiet archaeological site south of Madaba whose Church of St Stephen holds one of the Byzantine world's great mosaic floors, mapping the cities of the region, alongside a rare 15-metre stylite tower. An off-the-track gem for those who loved the Madaba map.

The ancient road threading Madaba, Wadi Mujib's canyon overlooks, Karak's Crusader castle and Dana on the scenic way south to Petra. With a private driver it turns the transfer into the journey — the slow, storied route rather than the fast desert highway.

A hulking Crusader fortress on a spur above the King's Highway, with vaulted halls and dungeons to explore and enormous valley views. A dramatic break on the drive to Petra that children and history-lovers both enjoy.

Jordan's 'Grand Canyon' meeting the Dead Sea — a wet gorge trail where you wade and scramble up a river between soaring walls, run by the RSCN in season. An exhilarating adventure for fit teenagers and adults, minutes from the Dead Sea resorts.

Thermal waterfalls tumbling steaming into pools in a desert gorge below sea level, with a spa resort built around them. A relaxing, slightly wild interlude near the Dead Sea, easy for all generations to enjoy.
A hidden speakeasy behind an unmarked door — the most serious, most awarded mixology in Jordan.
The original Rainbow Street rooftop — iconic three-hill views over downtown and a long, easy Amman evening.
A chic high-rise rooftop in the new downtown — inventive cocktails and a sweeping skyline panorama.
Open-air, junk-art rooftop that turns from supper to a lively late crowd over the lights of the old city.
